summary: The refutation is now receipt-backed. CheckRun f80378ddde474d69956d0df5d2e1a141 (completed, tests_passed, exit 0, 116 parsed observations, 0 parse errors) reproduces the decisive append operands at indices 63-64: node 2 appended the joint-enter removal of node 4 at index 2 with applied=1 and pendingConfIndex=0, then appended the joint-enter addition at index 4 with applied=3, pendingConfIndex=2 and joint_before=false while its own log already contained the joint-enter change at index 2. That combination cannot come from an application consuming its log in order - applying the change at index 2 makes a tracker joint - and it is the state the harness's restart event can produce by rebuilding a node with Config.Applied from its applied index while restoring the tracker from a ConfState written from the tracker rather than from the log that index covers. So the rejected history was produced by my restart modelling, not by the target's own producers, and with the receipt in hand I recorded the interpretation as explained with the defect claim refuted. I corrected the earlier knowledge entry that carried these operands as a draft-side note, changing its premise to observed-under-isolated-execution and narrowing its statement to the exact operands the receipt carries. What remains on record is what the receipts do establish: a JointImplicit change that alters no membership still creates a joint configuration needing a leave entry; that leave is proposed only by a node that is leader when it applies the change; in-order application of a joint-enter change on a joint configuration is rejected with 'config is already joint' and applyConfChange makes that process-fatal; and the propose-time check is best-effort by the target's own documentation with false negatives. That last point is the honest residue - a robustness boundary for callers who disable or defeat the check, or whose tracker state could legitimately go stale (a snapshot restore with a stale ConfState, for instance) - rather than an availability defect proved reachable through permitted operations in this snapshot. Limits recorded: the panicking path is documented behaviour rather than a discovery, the restarted-node path was not traced entry by entry so the attribution rests on the appender's impossible tracker state plus the harness's only mechanism for it, and storage faults, other cluster sizes, a rejecting leader and stale-ConfState snapshots remain outside the event set.
